subject: Climate & Environment
title: Cycling Cities
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Cycling Cities.

hook.text: Copenhagen aims to have more bikes than cars by 2025. They're almost there.

buildup.text: Protected bike lanes, traffic signals for cyclists, and flat terrain make cycling the obvious choice.

discovery.text: 62% of Copenhageners commute by bike. It saves the city millions in healthcare and road costs.

twist.text: Amsterdam wasn't always a cycling city. In the 1970s, it was clogged with cars. Citizens demanded change.

climax.text: Cities like Bogotá, Paris, and Barcelona are now building cycling networks inspired by Dutch success.

punchline.text: The most efficient vehicle ever invented has two wheels and no engine.

quiz.question: What percentage of Copenhagen residents commute by bicycle?

details.summary: Cities that invest in protected bike lanes, bike-sharing programs, and traffic-calmed streets see cycling rates surge. Cycling produces zero emissions, reduces congestion, costs cities far less than road infrastructure, and improves public health through physical activity.
details.whyItMatters: Cycling is the most energy-efficient form of transport. Making it safe and convenient transforms urban mobility while cutting emissions and improving quality of life.
takeaways: Protected bike lanes dramatically increase cycling rates
Cycling infrastructure costs a fraction of road building
Active transport improves public health and reduces emissions

faq.question: Which cities have the best cycling infrastructure?
faq.answer: Amsterdam and Copenhagen are the global leaders, with over 30 percent of trips made by bike. Utrecht, Strasbourg, and Bogota have also built extensive networks. In all cases, dedicated infrastructure and political commitment drove the shift.

faq.question: Can cycling work in hilly or hot cities?
faq.answer: Electric bicycles eliminate the barrier of hills and make cycling comfortable over longer distances and in warm climates. E-bike sales are booming globally and are expanding cycling to demographics and geographies that previously found it impractical.
